Abstract:Ensemble methods such as MeanQ have been shown to improve the sample efficiency of relatively small model-free deep reinforcement learning (RL) architectures, including DQN and similarly sized variants such as Rainbow. However, to our knowledge, the effects of ensembling on large-scale architectures such as Bigger Better Faster (BBF) have not been studied. In this work, we present MeanQ-BBF, a hybrid model-free algorithm that combines the principles of MeanQ and BBF. Through statistically rigorous evaluation on the Atari 100K benchmark, we show that in contrast to naive scaling of the network size of BBF, which degrades performance, MeanQ-BBF is able to leverage the increase in model capacity to improve performance over BBF. Moreover, MeanQ-BBF does this in a computationally efficient way by organizing the added parameters into largely independent learners. Finally, we discuss the performance-cost tradeoff in the context of practical sample-efficient RL.

Abstract:Software vulnerabilities persist as a critical threat despite the deployment of sophisticated detection tools and AI assistants. While detection has advanced, the subsequent code repair phase remains a primary bottleneck; manual intervention is inherently slow, costly, and prone to introducing secondary regressions and issues. In this paper, we investigate whether an iterative, LLM-based pipeline can provide a robust solution for the automated repair of vulnerable functions in real-world code. Abstract:Agnostic learning has a well-developed theory of computational and statistical complexity. For learning with distribution shift, even the choice of an appropriate error benchmark remains challenging. Testable learning with distribution shift (TDS) was introduced to develop computational foundations for this setting: using labeled training data and unlabeled test data, the learner must either produce a predictor with low test error or detect distribution shift. However, standard agnostic TDS guarantees allow a constant-factor amplification of the optimum error even when the training and test distributions coincide. They therefore do not directly recover the guarantee of classical agnostic learning. We introduce shift multiaccuracy, a stronger error benchmark inspired by multiaccuracy from algorithmic fairness. This yields a TDS formulation that becomes equivalent to multiaccuracy when there is no shift. Using a recent nontrivial reduction from agnostic learning to multiaccurate prediction from prior work, we obtain the first TDS framework that formally generalizes agnostic learning through an efficient reduction preserving the training marginal. The framework retains existing algorithmic upper bounds and inherits computational lower bounds from agnostic learning. Moreover, we establish a direct connection between our model and identity testing, yielding the first statistical characterization of agnostic TDS learning, in terms of Rademacher complexity. More broadly, we argue that shift multiaccuracy might be of independent interest in unsupervised domain adaptation, as it leads to sharper out-of-distribution generalization guarantees, and can be minimized directly, since its definition does not involve the unobserved test labels. Abstract:How much must a predictor’s scores change when a community’s elicited fairness standard changes? Similarity and tolerance judgments define protected comparisons and acceptable score gaps. For scores satisfying a source standard, we characterize the exact cost of retaining that standard during adaptation: runs of consecutive target constraints along shortest paths determine the optimal amplification factor. Its sharp worst case is \lfloor n/2\rfloor , and a full cost curve describes finite target-only repair budgets. Committing before the target is known can cost n-1 times the worst repair after revelation, even within one fixed convex ball of two-dimensional Mahalanobis metrics. Positive edge-budget floors cap both factors; bounded geometry also limits the commitment cost. At two interior targets of the construction attaining the n-1 bound, similarity queries alone yield a feasible 2 -approximate repair for tolerance \eps\le1/[2(n-1)] , reducing movement relative to common repair by a factor linear in n . Feasible (1+\alpha) -optimal repair on this family has worst-case tolerance-query complexity \Theta(\alpha^-2n^2\log(1/\delta)) under a fixed-slope logistic model. Abstract:Learning from limited target data is a central challenge in cross-domain offline reinforcement learning. Abundant source data can help, but dynamics differences can make direct transition reuse unreliable. We propose Reward Improvement Field Transfer (RIFT), which instead learns how low- and high-reward source transitions differ. RIFT encodes source and target transitions in a shared latent space, pairs low- and high-reward source transitions using optimal transport, and fits an affine field to their displacements. It applies this field to low-reward target anchors and decodes the results to augment the target dataset. Abstract:Stochastic closure modeling is an emerging area in reduced-order modeling of large and complex (e.g., multiscale, multi-physics) systems, for which the computationally affordable reduced-order physical descriptions (e.g., digital twins for additive manufacturing, world models for AI agents) in numerical simulations inevitably lead to information losses that cannot be well addressed by classical deterministic closures. However, learning stochastic closures typically requires closure data that are difficult to obtain from measurements or often prohibitively expensive to compute using first-principles simulations. In this work, we develop a stochastic closure modeling framework that builds on score-based diffusion models, leveraging indirect offline training and online data assimilation without requiring the direct data of closures. Numerical experiments on two-dimensional turbulent flows demonstrate that indirect offline learning captures key closure statistics and improves predictions of system state. In addition, combining the learned closure with known physical dynamics leads to better generalization capability across different regimes than purely data-driven models that directly predict system state. Compared to standard data assimilation methods with a Gaussian assumption, the posterior-score assimilation better represents non-Gaussian features of the learned closure, and its combination with state-level data assimilation further improves prediction of the system state. The proposed framework enables stochastic closure modeling in realistic and challenging scenarios of complex dynamical systems in mechanics and engineering problems, where non-Gaussian statistics of model-form uncertainties are non-negligible (e.g., due to the nonlinearities of the system dynamics and/or the observations) and true closure data are not available, for both offline learning and online assimilation.

Abstract:Molecular dynamics (MD) simulations can capture the nanoscale physics of fracture at the atomistic level, but their computational cost prohibits predictions at the length scales and time scales needed for many applications. Machine learning approaches, on the other hand, have been proposed as heuristic surrogates for material fracture, yet they cannot guarantee the physical consistency of the predicted response. To address this shortcoming, we propose the mesoscale neural operator (MNO): a data-driven nonlocal constitutive model that is learned directly from MD loading and displacement data. After training, it can be used in continuum fracture simulations on much larger domains and grid sizes. The key idea of the MNO is to exploit the built-in characteristic length of a nonlocal model, called the horizon, to travel across scales. Physical consistency across scales is obtained by building two structural ingredients into the MNO: a normalized kernel that renders the strain energy density invariant under horizon rescaling, and a rescaled critical bond stretch that keeps the energy release rate consistent across scales. Through tests on synthetic data, we show that the MNO and its learning workflow indeed discover the nonlocal continuum multiscale model in the form of the nonlocal kernel and the nonlinear constitutive relation. We then apply the framework to coarse-grained MD data and find that in a test problem, the learned model matches the MD strain energy density and critical energy release rate within 3%. As a further demonstration, the model is applied to a plate with 4000 times the area of the training specimens and containing an initial defect. In this problem, the model reproduces the main features of dynamic brittle fracture, including branch and cascading branch networks.

Abstract:Modeling olfactory mixtures remains a critical challenge in machine olfaction because the task requires reasoning over relationships between sets of odorants rather than over individual molecules in isolation. Abstract:Many decision-making problems involve multiple objectives, where actions affect several performance metrics, fairness criteria, or safety constraints. Existing approaches to multi-objective bandits often rely on pairwise Pareto dominance or optimize a fixed scalarization. However, pairwise comparisons alone can fail to identify actions dominated by randomized policies, whose expected reward vectors lie in the convex hull of action-level rewards. Thus, an intervention may be suboptimal even if no single intervention dominates it, because it can be dominated by a randomized policy over other interventions. We formalize this policy-level phenomenon and show that it has consequences for both causal action-space reduction and online learning. First, we provide a necessary-and-sufficient graphical characterization of possibly Pareto- optimal minimal intervention sets. Our characterization yields a minimal, sound, and complete candidate intervention family from the graph alone, correcting prior formulations that may include intervention sets that are never Pareto-optimal under any compatible structural causal model. Second, over this reduced intervention space, we design an online UCB-style algorithm that eliminates actions using dominance tests against convex combinations of other actions, and prove logarithmic gap-dependent Pareto regret. Finally, we study constrained multi-objective causal bandits, where feasibility and optimality may be realized only with randomized policies, and develop an online UCB-style constrained bandit algorithm with sublinear regret and constraint-violation guarantees.

Abstract:Learning the underlying probability distribution from samples is a core problem in statistics and applied mathematics. Generative models based on diffusion and flow matching learn a velocity field whose flow transports a known distribution to the data distribution. They produce novel, realistic samples, although the empirical learning problem is ill posed near the data distribution. Its minimizer transports the samples onto the training data, and small perturbations of the data change the velocity field strongly near the end of the flow. The observed generalization is often attributed to implicit regularization by the network parameterization, early stopping of the training, and the time integration during sampling. Explicit regularization has advanced the theory and computation of many inverse problems and has recently been proposed to prevent memorization in generative models. With a regularizer on the magnitude of the velocity, however, the field approaches the memorizing velocity unless the regularization parameter grows to infinity fast enough, and it then stays bounded by a constant that is small only for large parameters. We show that penalizing the derivatives of order k of the velocity renders the D -dimensional empirical problem well posed uniformly in time if 2k D and the training points are in general position. Our experiments in one and two dimensions discretize the velocity with splines and use direct solvers for the regularized least-squares problems to exclude optimization error. Refining the discretization in space and time changes the error of the Hessian-regularized flows only marginally, whereas without the regularizer the error tends to that of memorization. These flows generalize, with errors comparable to or lower than those of well-tuned kernel density estimates.

Abstract:Accurate time series forecasting with exogenous inputs is critical across domains, including energy and retail, yet modern deep learning models often overfit to correlations that do not generalize under shifts in these inputs. We propose SLiDE, a Koopman-inspired architecture for forecasting with exogenous inputs that imposes structure on latent temporal dynamics. SLiDE approximates nonlinear system evolution using a learned linear operator in a latent space, combining (i) a history encoder that reconstructs the current latent state from past targets and inputs with (ii) a shared linear rollout driven by future exogenous variables. By enforcing a common linear recurrence across encoding and prediction, SLiDE aligns how past information is encoded with how future states evolve, reducing parameterization and preventing reliance on spurious correlations in the input history. Empirically, SLiDE achieves state-of-the-art accuracy on real-world benchmarks, including electricity price forecasting and retail demand, while maintaining a computational footprint comparable to lightweight MLP architectures. SLiDE is especially effective at generalizing to shifted exogenous inputs, reducing MSE by 20% on electricity price samples with out-of-range exogenous values and MAE by 30% in a synthetic transfer setting where the same dynamical system is driven by an unseen exogenous process. Ablations confirm the importance of both the structured history encoder and the linear latent rollout, suggesting that structured latent linear dynamics provide a useful inductive bias for forecasting with exogenous inputs.

Abstract:Just as the data in a dynamic stream changes, questions asked of the stream also change in intent: what to hold constant, which counterfactuals to consider, and so forth. Energy-based learning has been celebrated for its uniform approach to losses and estimation, but interpretability remains challenging. Tree-based methods, on the other hand, offer high interpretability but often rely on bespoke, disjointed estimators. Neither paradigm readily supports changing questions on streaming data. In this paper we take a step towards combining energy, interpretability, and streaming. Random cut forests retain an evolving geometry of the data. We study this geometry as the basis for diffusion dynamics, prediction, explanation, and games. We show that several existing scores are escape probabilities of random walks on the trees. The induced affinity is realized exactly by a sparse electrical network on each tree, giving a single energy calculus, a Hamiltonian, maintained along one path per update. This connects an estimate, its supporting evidence, and the response to intervention through the same boxes, gaps, masses, and paths. Different questions correspond to different clamp decisions on the energy. Fixing observed values gives harmonic prediction with Gaussian uncertainty. Fixing a partition gives normalized cuts whose cost is attributed exactly to oriented faces. Releasing clamps gives coalition games, in which collusive displacement measures the field response. With noise, the same energy gives diffusion dynamics whose relaxation rates are read from the boxes. Axis-parallel cuts localize at a rate set by affine rather than ambient dimension, and this control passes to the averaged energy. Across a forest the boxes are only approximately nested; common reference observations align the trees. A rotating star with added noise illustrates the measurements. Abstract:Sharpness Aware Minimization (SAM) updates model parameters using gradients evaluated at adversarially perturbed weights, but it remains unclear which aspects of this procedure are sufficient to reproduce its generalization behavior. In our ResNet 18 experiments on CIFAR 10, simple curvature regularizers based on the Hessian trace and largest eigenvalue remain below SAM in validation accuracy, motivating a direct examination of its perturbations. We introduce statistical replay, a diagnostic that summarizes perturbations from reference SAM trajectories using elementwise means and standard deviations over local windows and constructs new perturbations during independent SGD training. Pure replay uses only these summaries, whereas mixed replay adds isotropic Gaussian noise. Pure replay does not reproduce SAM’s validation behavior, while mixed replay and pure isotropic perturbations can approach its validation performance at selected scales without reproducing its training dynamics. Abstract:During grokking, a network transitions from memorization to generalization, yet what shapes the neural implementation (circuit) of the generalizing solution and specifically the number of participating neurons (its size) remains unclear. We find that the learning rule, the combination of credit assignment algorithm and optimizer, controls this: On modular addition, every learning rule we study that groks recovers the same Fourier-based algorithm, yet implemented by circuits that differ in size. Why? A neuron stays in use when its credit is large relative to the non-gradient term of its own update, and this single condition unifies three routes to unused neurons: the coupled weight decay, Adam’s \epsilon and the decay of a trainable per-neuron gain. Equalizing the magnitude of credit assigned to each neuron, or scaling each neuron’s weight decay by its credit, expands the effective circuit size, measured from the outgoing weights, from 60% to 99% of the layer’s neurons at similar training and test accuracy. We vary which neurons share one equalization factor, from the whole layer to individual neurons, and find that the circuit stays concentrated for groups of eight or more and fully distributes only when every neuron has its own factor. Credit magnitudes are usually set by the normalization of standard optimizers: Nero, which normalizes per neuron, distributes the computation, whereas Adam and seven others, including RMSProp, Muon, and Shampoo, use other normalization schemes and retain small, concentrated circuits. Distributed circuits tolerate neuron deletion better, while concentrated circuits can be pruned further and transfer about twice as fast to a task that recombines the same features, largely by recruiting their unused neurons. Learning rule choice thus steers circuit size, trading robustness against compressibility and transfer speed without changing the learned algorithm.

Abstract:World models learned from offline data allow an agent to plan without further interaction with the environment, but the sampling-based planners used with them handle safety constraints only by scoring or rejecting sampled action sequences. We instead pose safe planning in the latent space of a learned world model as a successive convex program (SCP), in which a learned discrete-time control barrier function is imposed as a constraint at every step of the horizon. SCP requires smooth dynamics, so we build the networks from smoothed MaxMin activations and spectrally normalised layers, and bound the resulting linearisation error in terms of the Lipschitz bound and the smoothing width. As SCP is a local method, we start it from a sampled plan. On two Safety-Gymnasium navigation tasks with offline data, this planner has fewer violations than MPPI and CEM drawing 128 times as many samples at equal wall-clock time in our main comparison, though not significantly, and earns greater return at longer horizons, and is much safer than SCP without a sampled start. SCP converged more often on Lipschitz-bounded models. Unlike sampling, it also reports at each step whether its plan is a feasible, first-order optimal KKT point of the planning problem in the model, or that no feasible plan was found nearby. Our implementation is publicly available at this https URL.

Abstract:Heimdall, a learned controller, calls slow on 52% of an SSD’s reads when 30% are slow. Uncertainty estimators, the remedy prescribed for its wrong guesses, cannot find them: nine of them do no better than a coin. The drive can. On one trace, 2% of the reads of 4 to 8 KiB that found less than 4 KiB outstanding while the drive was answering came back slow, and Heimdall called 96% of them slow. A 4,096-entry table of how the drive’s recent reads came back, untrained and 21 ns a decision, ranks the wrong guesses at a median AUROC of 0.68 on 57 held-out traces, where the nine sit at 0.46 to 0.52, and it predicts slow reads better than Heimdall itself.

Abstract:Causal validation of training data attribution (TDA) methods is costly, since evaluation involves retraining a model on many different subsets of the original training set. For example, the Linear Datamodeling Score (LDS), which has become a standard metric for evaluating TDA methods, measures the correlation between TDA predictions and expected retrained model outputs. In this paper, we reduce the amount of computation needed to estimate the LDS along three axes: the number of sampled training subsets, the number of retraining seeds per subset, and the number of models in the attribution ensemble. Each of these factors induces a form of bias in the LDS estimation, and removing these sources of bias significantly reduces the number of retrainings needed to match the same accuracy in LDS estimation. On ResNet-9/CIFAR-10, finite-subset debiasing achieves 3.2% relative RMSE with as few as 4 subsets, and 32 subsets match the accuracy of ordinary Spearman using 96 subsets, measured against a 300-subset reference. On ResNet-9/CIFAR-10, BERT/QNLI and GPT-2/WikiText-2, estimating the training-noise variance allows us to reproduce the standard five-seed LDS at the same accuracy with 2 – 5\times fewer retrainings.

Abstract:Depth recurrence increases effective model depth by repeatedly applying a fixed computation block. However, sharing attention parameters does not share the key-value (KV) states generated at different recurrence iterations, which causes memory growth with recurrence depth during autoregressive decoding. We study how to reduce this memory cost through architectural and cache-sharing approaches within a common depth-recurrent framework. We first study a looped hybrid that repeats a stack of Transformer layers, with recurrent mLSTM or Gated DeltaNet blocks replacing most attention layers and periodic Transformer attention anchors retained. We then restrict recurrence to a dedicated recurrent workspace in a Parcae-style architecture and test its stabilising adapter as a wrapper for the looped hybrid. Finally, we train a looped Transformer with recurrent KV replay, where only selected recurrence iterations write KV states that later iterations reuse. This trains the model to operate with the same shared KV topology used during inference. We find that looped hybrids require sufficiently frequent attention anchors, with performance depending strongly on the recurrent mixer. For cross-iteration KV sharing, recurrent KV replay allows multiple recurrence iterations to reuse the same KV states while retaining performance close to the full looped Transformer with separate KV caches for each iteration.

Abstract:Background: Photovoltaic (PV) forecasts inform energy commitments by PV operators and aggregators and guide charge-discharge scheduling in solar-plus-storage systems. Federated learning enables collaborative model training through model updates when local operators cannot pool raw operational data. This study evaluated whether federated training was non-inferior to centralized training for PV capacity-factor prediction across seven stations in North Macedonia. A common multilayer perceptron was used in an offline forecasting comparison with a 24-hour timestamp lag. Exploratory validation compared local, centralized, Federated Averaging, and Federated Proximal (FedProx) training. FedProx (E = 1, mu = 1) was selected for a confirmatory comparison under a protocol fixed before test evaluation. The comparison used past-only offline inputs, five paired training seeds, macro-averaged mean absolute error (MAE), a prespecified non-inferiority margin of 0.005, and a paired day bootstrap with 10,000 repetitions over 49 test dates. Results: FedProx achieved a macro-MAE of 0.128397, compared with 0.133405 for centralized training. The paired difference (FedProx minus centralized) was -0.005008 (95% confidence interval: [-0.009926, -0.000537]). The upper confidence bound was below the prespecified margin, satisfying the non-inferiority criterion. All five seed-specific differences favored FedProx, and its mean MAE was lower at six of the seven stations. Post hoc calendar sensitivity analyses did not change the conclusion. Conclusions: These findings support further evaluation of federated forecasting for collaboration under data-pooling constraints. The study demonstrates predictive non-inferiority within the evaluated setting. Benefits for energy commitments and battery scheduling remain potential applications requiring operational evaluation. Abstract:Diffusion models can learn multimodal distributions over finite-horizon state-input sequences, providing a way to generate candidates for predictive control. However, sequences generated by a pretrained model may violate safety constraints introduced at deployment, for example when obstacles are added or repositioned. Retraining whenever these constraints change limits the usefulness of learned predictive controllers. In this paper, we propose Test-Time Constraint-Aware Diffusion Predictive Control (TCA-DPC), an algorithm for adapting the sampling distribution of a pretrained diffusion controller to newly introduced safety constraints without retraining. We treat the pretrained model as a prior over finite-horizon sequences and define an adapted distribution through exponential tilting based on a constraint-violation penalty. The tilt strength is adjusted online using the fraction of generated sequences that fail constraint verification. We approximately sample the adapted distribution using the Metropolis-adjusted Langevin algorithm in the Gaussian noise space of the pretrained diffusion sampler.

[LG-130] β-number and Its Applications to Data Science

作者: Pengxu Wen,Ziwei Nie,Liwen Zou,Ying Cao,Xiaoping Yang

Abstract:In this paper, we introduce a novel metric, \beta -number, designed to measure the " p -th order d -dimensional oscillation degree" of a set. For a given set K in the Euclidean space \mathbbR^n , \beta -number is computed by identifying an optimal d -dimensional plane L that minimizes the average p -th order distance of all points in K to L . This metric serves as a versatile tool in data science, functioning both as a dimensionality reduction technique to find the optimal p -th order d -dimensional subspace and as a measure to characterize data oscillation for classification. We conduct a thorough exploration of \beta -number through theoretical analysis and numerical experiments. Initially, we establish the upper and lower bounds of \beta -number for any set K , along with its scaling law. We then elucidate the relationships between \beta -number and its related parameters. A key finding of this study is that in discrete settings, when p=2 , the d -dimensional plane determined by \beta -number coincides with that obtained via Principal Component Analysis (PCA), positioning \beta -number as a generalization of PCA. Furthermore, we propose two algorithms for calculating \beta -number in both continuous and discrete settings. We validate our theoretical results through a series of numerical experiments in low-dimensional cases. Finally, we demonstrate the potential of \beta -number in practical data analysis through a dimensionality reduction task and an image classification task.

[LG-131] Enforcing Ellipsoidal Constraints in Neural Networks with a Polynomial Safety Layer

作者: Rolf Findeisen,Sebastian Hirt,Hoang Hai Nguyen,Grace Li Zhang,Hendrik Alsmeier
类目: ystems and Control (eess.SY); Machine Learning (cs.LG); Optimization and Control (math.OC)

Abstract:Often the output of a learned mapping must satisfy prescribed constraints. In the control of autonomous systems, for example, the chosen action must keep the system within a collision-free region. We consider the case in which a proposed output is corrected by projection onto a safety ellipsoid. Computing this projection amounts to solving a quadratically constrained quadratic program (QCQP). We construct a neural-network safety layer by unrolling a feasibility-preserving polynomial penalty iteration. The unrolled structure allows the loss gradient to propagate from the feasible output through the safety layer to the network parameters during training. We show how to choose the layer parameters so that every iterate is feasible and give a computable bound on its distance to the exact projection at any prescribed depth. We illustrate the method by training a LiDAR-based policy to control an unmanned aerial vehicle. A privileged model predictive control expert uses the map and the measured vehicle state to generate the training data. In the simulated narrow mazes, the filtered policy avoided wall contact at every tested stage of training, including at initialization, when every unfiltered flight hit a wall. A representative build of the learned policy and its safety layer for an Arm Cortex-M4F microcontroller occupies about 36 KiB of flash, with a RAM budget below 5 KiB.

[LG-132] Gradient-Based Co-Design of Systems and Reinforcement Learning Policies with Differentiable Simulators

链接: https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.19329
作者: Akhil S. Anand,Xun Shen,Marc Peter Deisenroth,Sebastien Gros
类目: Machine Learning (cs.LG); Systems and Control (eess.SY); Optimization and Control (math.OC)
*备注: 31 pages, 5 figures, 3 tables

点击查看摘要

Abstract:Co-design is the problem of jointly optimizing the design of a system and the policy that operates it. Neither can be chosen independently: a system design is only as good as the policy trained for it, and the optimal policy changes with the design. When that policy is learned by reinforcement learning (RL), evaluating a candidate design requires a full policy training run, and the design is usually optimized by black-box search such as Bayesian optimization (BO) or evolution strategies (ES). These methods scale poorly with the design dimension and ignore the differentiable structure of modern simulators and, in particular, the sensitivity of the optimal policy with respect to the design. We instead derive a gradient-based co-design method, where the design gradient decomposes into a direct effect of changing the design at a fixed policy and an indirect effect through the design-dependent optimal policy. The indirect effect requires the sensitivity of the converged policy to the design, which we obtain by applying the implicit function theorem to the stationarity condition of the policy gradient. Based on this sensitivity, we develop a proof-of-concept co-design algorithm with stochastic value gradient (SVG)-style policy optimization, prove that it converges to an approximately stationary design, and demonstrate on a differentiable networked-system benchmark with high-dimensional design spaces that it consistently outperforms BO and ES.

Abstract:A backdoored language model behaves normally until a trigger phrase appears in its input. Every published method for recovering such a trigger runs the model. We show the trigger is legible in the weights alone: a static statistic reads a fine-tuned checkpoint with no forward pass of the suspect, no data, no labelled population of poisoned models and no prior knowledge that a backdoor exists, and names one of the tokens of the trigger phrase as the single highest-ranked candidate in the vocabulary.

Abstract:Does readily available lifestyle information improve machine-learning prediction of hypertension beyond routine demographic and anthropometric data? On NHANES 2017-March 2020, five model families (Logistic Regression, Random Forest, Gradient Boosting, Bagged Decision Trees, and XGBoost) were evaluated with fold-local preprocessing and paired bootstrap confidence intervals. Adding physical activity, alcohol use, smoking, and sleep information showed no consistent detectable improvement in held-out discrimination: every paired ROC-AUC confidence interval included zero, including under a stricter measured-blood-pressure phenotype and without synthetic oversampling. Mean cross-model SHAP rank agreement fell from 0.873 to 0.806 over all encoded columns, but this decline was largely attenuated over the 19 baseline columns shared by both arms (0.873 vs. 0.863), and likewise under both robustness checks; attribution-agreement comparisons across feature sets of different sizes therefore require a matched comparison space. In exploratory analysis of untreated adults (measured-blood-pressure outcome), all five models showed small positive differences, two with unadjusted intervals excluding zero, meriting confirmation. These results do not imply that lifestyle factors are clinically unimportant; within this cohort, the evaluated lifestyle block added little incremental discrimination beyond an already-informative baseline.

Abstract:Network dismantling seeks to fragment a network with as few node removals as possible, which is widely applied in vulnerability analysis, epidemic containment, and infrastructure protection. Although learning-based methods have become increasingly prominent, their progress remains difficult to assess because existing studies differ in method coverage, datasets, evaluation criteria, and experimental protocols. Thus, we introduce NetBreaker, a comprehensive benchmark designed for the learning era of network dismantling. NetBreaker organizes 30 methods (18 non-learning and 12 learning-based) under a common taxonomy and evaluates them on 185 networks from eight unified domains, ranging from 14 to 1.69 million nodes. To enable fair comparison, heterogeneous method outputs are converted into node removal sequences and assessed under a unified execution protocol. The evaluation covers four complementary dimensions: target-based effectiveness, trajectory-based effectiveness, structural diagnostics, and applicability computational efficiency. Extensive experiments show that current learningbased methods do not consistently outperform strong non-learning approaches, while exposing substantial differences in effectiveness, scalability, and efficiency across network conditions and evaluation perspectives. NetBreaker provides a reproducible basis for measuring progress and developing reliable, scalable, and computationally efficient network dismantling methods.

Abstract:An electronic nose must name every ingredient of a mixture, including combinations it has never measured. SmellNet, a public benchmark for this task, scores ingredients with a hit rate that is told how many each sample contains. We audit what this protocol hides. We hold out ingredient combinations from the SmellNet training data, evaluate four architectures (MLP, CNN, LSTM and a Transformer encoder) without revealing the ingredient count, and repeat the evaluation once on the official unseen split. Under the count-informed protocol, 90-96% of mixtures receive an ingredient that is absent, on our folds and on the official split alike. On our folds, every model identifies one ingredient reliably but the second rarely, and it completes the pair with a familiar training partner about twice as often as chance. On the official split, even the first-ranked ingredient is correct in only 29-46% of binary mixtures, often because a frequent training ingredient that is absent from every test pair is ranked first, and on its combinations that are truly absent from training no model names both ingredients in more than 1.2% of them. The failures fall on the same ingredients for every architecture, and a frequency correction only moves errors between ingredients. Mixture recognition is therefore limited by ingredients the models cannot separate and by a preference for frequent ingredients, not by the architecture, and it should be evaluated with set-level errors and without oracle cardinality.

Abstract:Crowdsourcing has emerged as a promising paradigm for constructing AI services by harnessing the collective capabilities of distributed workers. As consumers’ demands continually evolve, service models must acquire new knowledge while retaining previously learned information. However, due to the inherited reliance on gradients for backpropagation, existing approaches typically suffer from catastrophic forgetting during continual model updates on heterogeneous data. Recent studies have introduced analytic learning, a gradient-free paradigm that achieves invariance through recursive closed-form solutions. Nevertheless, existing analytic methods are typically constrained by single-layer linear networks, which tend to suffer from underfitting due to their inability to perform deep representation learning. To address this issue, we propose ReCALM, a Residual-enhanced Crowdsourced Analytic Learning Mechanism that achieves deep nonlinear invariance for distributed continual service construction. Inspired by the success of ResNet, we develop gradient-free residual blocks for ReCALM with closed-form solutions. To implement distributed continual training for ReCALM, we further devise a cross-recursive strategy via least squares. Both theoretical and experimental analyses verify ReCALM’s dual superiority in heterogeneity invariance and deep representation. With 20 residual layers, ReCALM improves accuracy by 8.85%-9.83% over the single-layer analytic baseline, while reducing computational costs by over 94% compared with gradient-based baselines.

Abstract:Reasoning about what an action will cause requires internalizing how a system behaves. As conditions seldom stay fixed, this must often happen within a few interactions. Yet systems that look identical in a snapshot can respond differently to the same action, depending on physical conditions the snapshot hides. Context-based models capture this separation by summarizing recent transitions into a latent context, but do not specify how that context should change the equations of motion. Physics-informed neural networks build those equations into the model, but describe only a single system and cannot recognize when it has changed. We present Physics-Informed Causal Reasoning (PICR), which bridges the two. Only a context, re-inferred from recent interactions, is updated; it conditions a fixed physics-informed network that determines the robot’s inertia and potential energy, so the robot adapts to new physical conditions from its own experience without retraining or a hand-specified robot model. On a Franka Panda arm in NVIDIA Isaac Sim, PICR predicts motion under changing and unseen payloads, reducing error on the latter by 1.6-3.8x over baselines, and extends to counterfactual queries under alternative torques. Our analysis shows that the context, inferred solely from interaction, encodes payload physical properties, tracks their changes, and governs the arm’s response. The gravity and inertia terms induced by the context further demonstrate its physical validity, each agreeing with the simulator at the level of individual Lagrangian components.

Abstract:The same node attributes can imply different labels in different structural contexts. Yet fast graphless models typically treat topology as additional evidence supplied to a globally shared predictor. This assumes that structure augments the available information, rather than determining how node attributes should be interpreted. We introduce SCOPE (Structure-COnditioned PrEdictor), in which a small generator maps each node’s cached structural fingerprint to coefficients over a shared low-rank basis, producing a context-specific update to a global weight matrix. The base predictor, basis, and generator remain shared across all nodes, while the resulting transformation adapts how attributes are processed in each relational environment. Once fingerprints are cached, inference requires only a forward pass and no online message passing. This design combines context-specific specialization with global parameter sharing, compact low-rank adaptation, and message-passing-free inference. On two large OGB node-classification graphs, conditioning the weights with raw positional signals yields clear gains over supplying the same signals through input concatenation. Further results under a structure-transductive held-out-node protocol and in teacher-free graph classification show that the mechanism extends beyond a particular distillation setting. These findings establish graph structure not only as predictive evidence, but as context that determines the predictor used to interpret that evidence.

Abstract:Intent-driven exoskeleton control needs a continuous, causal estimate of the wearer’s joint kinematics and an answer to a second question: whose data should train the estimator for a new user? Borrowing the user’s recordings of other activities, or other users’ recordings of the same activity, is usually evaluated as “more data” versus “less data,” which confounds the information a source carries with the optimizer updates it adds and hides negative transfer behind averages. We separate these effects for hip, knee, and ankle angle estimation from high-density sEMG and an IMU across six locomotion activities on all ten participants of a public dataset. A compact residual causal TCN-GRU decoder is frozen, and an update-matched replay control prices every added source against the same number of updates on the user’s own data. A user’s own other activities raise R^2 from 0.722 to 0.788, of which +0.048 is information beyond replay; stair descent is a reliably harmful donor and sit-stand-walk a reliably beneficial one. Other users’ same-activity data help while the user has only the target activity ( G_\mathrmT = +0.053 ) and half as much once own other-activity data exist ( G_\mathrmW = +0.028 ); at full calibration, donor value collapses after one to two target records. Abstract:There is growing interest in foundation models (FMs) for power grids, particularly for power flow and optimal power flow. Their usefulness depends on generalization accuracy, which existing works test on their own benchmarks. We propose a three-axis framework to test their generalization limits: changed admittance matrices of training grids, load levels, and unseen grids. We test GENCO, LUMINA and GridSFM against the DC baseline, alongside their reported limitations, and discuss theoretical reasons for their failures. Experiments reveal that adding a line degrades all FMs more than removing one, and longer lines eventually make LUMINA and fine-tuned GENCO worse than DC. All three degrade beyond their training load range, where the loading-voltage curve steepens. On unseen grids, LUMINA degrades sharply even inside its training range, and GridSFM fails on the grid farthest from it. Thus, beyond training conditions, FMs behave more like meta-models requiring test-time fine-tuning data and compute.

Abstract:Recovering the forces behind a motion is ill-posed: different controllers can reproduce the same movement while generating different contact forces. Physics-based motion imitation resolves this ambiguity through simulation, but relies on fixed-gain proportional-derivative (PD) control. We show that fixed gains impose a trade-off between motion and force tracking, as contact and swing place conflicting demands on joint stiffness and damping. We introduce ImpedanceMimic, a reinforcement-learning policy that modulates per-joint stiffness, damping, and position setpoints from motion and force measurements, but requires only motion at inference. Across 129 participants and six activities, ImpedanceMimic outperforms matched fixed-gain PD under every integration scheme, direct-torque, muscle-actuated and existing imitation controllers in kinematic and force fidelity, approaching a dedicated motion-to-force regressor. By expressing gains as multiples of inertia-scaled priors, a single policy controls subject-specific biomechanical models without explicit anthropometric input and transfers zero-shot to unseen humans and a humanoid robot. The learned impedance forms a low-dimensional representation of motor state, shared across bodies, that generalizes to withheld activities: stiffness scales with load, and damping anticipates unloading.

Abstract:The Apple Neural Engine (ANE) is in over a billion devices, but is characterized indirectly via CoreML. Using a CoreML-free fused-graph dispatch path, we measure the ANE, along with the Apple GPU and CPU on the same device, with per-engine energy accounting. The consumer-available roofline does not predict the ANE in practice. A critical correction is that the ANE sees two effective memory bandwidths: a slow activation path and a fast weight-stream path. Two roofline ridges follow, and the weight-stream ridge is below that of the GPU. The ANE single-operand compute peak decreases instead of plateauing. Its weight stream is byte-bound in fp16 but limited by the dequantizer’s element rate in int8. As a result, int8 compression saves energy at unchanged throughput and an int4 lookup-table stream raises throughput and efficiency at a cost of 2.55 points of ImageNet top-1. The corrected roofline identifies the lower-energy ANE paths and bounds it from below. A constructed device map reproduces across four unique ANE generations. Results show that operators should be placed by arithmetic intensity and fused for optimal performance.

Abstract:Static Code Analysis (SCA) tools are vital for software development to reduce the cost and time required for manual code reviews. Several approaches have been taken in existing studies to identify false-positive alarms generated by SCA tools, in helping to enhance the utility of these tools. However, existing studies reveal several limitations, chiefly among which is the tendency to focus on a limited number of alarm types or failing to evaluate a large breadth of Machine-Learning (ML) techniques comprehensively. This study has addressed this opportunity. Abstract:The familywise (FW) loss for multiclass classification, introduced by Duchi, Ruan, and Khosravi, achieves universal equivalence to the 0-1 loss, and thus has stronger theoretical properties than cross entropy (CE). Prior work, however, left open whether FW is as computationally efficient as CE. First, on the theoretical side, we prove that the FW gradient can be computed in O(K) time, where K is the number of classes. Second, on the practical side, we develop optimized kernels for computing the forward and backward passes of FW which outperform CE in terms of speed on both CPU and GPU.

Abstract:Diffusion policies, which generate short action sequences by denoising random noise, are a leading way to learn robot skills from demonstrations. Once deployed, they meet constraints the demonstrations never contained, and retraining for each is impractical. A safety filter edits the policy’s action to satisfy them, but the edit ignores the task, and a large edit can leave the policy where it cannot continue. We propose CAST (Certified Action Selection at Test time): draw a few action chunks from the frozen policy, certify each with a barrier condition, and execute the certified chunk that a learned value ensemble ranks highest. We prove that a certified step is safe whatever the critic does; that, whenever a certified sample exists, the executed chunk stays within log N nats of the policy conditioned on feasibility, while a safety-filter projection can be singular to it; and that an exact closed-loop identity splits the gain of ranking into availability, spread and the critic’s target. Certifying the next chunk is not enough: a generative controller can have safe actions available now and none later. We characterise the safe control authority of a frozen policy under finite sampling, and CAST-V preserves it through a policy-conditioned viability, estimated with a model under a finite-sample guarantee or learned from the controller’s own logs (CAST-VL). On robomimic manipulation, a planar quadrotor, a MuJoCo humanoid and a unicycle, with frozen policies, CAST raises joint task-and-constraint success above the output filter in nearly every setting; certifying before ranking is decisive where a filter’s edit is large, and viability removes most dead ends that one-step certification cannot see. Abstract:The importance of reliable uncertainty estimation in large language models (LLMs) has become increasingly pronounced, yet modern models remain poorly calibrated and frequently overconfident. In this study, we address this by proposing an efficient method for LLM classifier calibration using the Asymmetric Duos framework. Our approach combines a strong base model with a smaller sidekick model via logit-space fusion, utilizing global scaling parameters optimized on a validation set. Across diverse benchmarks, this Asymmetric LLM Duo consistently achieves best or second-best performance on expected calibration error and negative log-likelihood, without degrading predictive accuracy. More importantly, these gains are realized at a fraction of the computational cost of more complex baselines, placing our method on the calibration-compute Pareto frontier. We further demonstrate that our method acts orthogonal to various established calibration-aware techniques, meaning it can be easily combined with them to consistently boost their performance. Finally, our analysis of the logit-space behavior illustrates how asymmetric fusion successfully mitigates base model overconfidence. Overall, our findings demonstrate that the benefits of an asymmetric fusion successfully transfer to the language domain, providing a simple, highly cost-efficient approach to improving uncertainty estimation in LLM classifiers.

Abstract:Large Language Models (LLMs) have been known to exhibit a wide range of social biases including name-nationality associations, occupation-gender associations and racial stereotypes. Existing approaches to evaluating these biases typically involve measuring surface-level behavior where a model is fed a dataset of prompts and its outputs are scored relative to ground-truth answers. Inspired by prior elicitation in cognitive science, we propose a different perspective that reconstructs latent bias as a prior underlying the model’s behavior. We formulate the problem as a Bayesian inverse problem where, given prompt-response observations on a bias benchmark dataset, we infer a low-dimensional latent distribution that summarizes the model’s stereotyping tendencies. This paper develops the mathematical foundation, a practical reconstruction algorithm, and experiments using the Bias Benchmark for QA (BBQ) benchmark to infer the prior distributions of LLMs over responses in ambiguous social contexts.

作者: Kazi Ashik Islam,Guojing Cong

Abstract:Sequence models represent past context at different resolutions, using token-level keys and values, fixed-size recurrent states, or hierarchies of compressed summaries. Full attention supports strong associative recall but requires quadratic work during training and prefill and a linearly growing key-value cache during inference. Linear attention and state-space models reduce these costs through fixed-size recurrent memory, but this compression can limit recall. Log-linear attention offers a middle ground by maintaining logarithmically many state matrices. However, its hierarchy favors finer resolution near the current query while compressing earlier context into coarser summaries. To complement this allocation of resolution, we introduce bilateral log-linear attention, which pairs the existing hierarchy with a second hierarchy anchored at the sequence origin. By combining their reads, the two branches provide finer access to both early and recent context while remaining causal. We derive recurrent and chunkwise parallel formulations for the added branch, preserving log-linear training and prefill work, logarithmic decoding work per token, and logarithmic persistent state storage at fixed feature dimensions and chunk size. In multi-query associative recall, this design raises mean overall test accuracy from 76.37% to 96.12% over forward log-linear attention across multiple training seeds. For pretrained language models under approximate parameter matching, it raises the mean score on six selected RULER needle-in-a-haystack tasks from 26.97% to 50.03% at a context length of 6144 tokens. In the same setting, bilateral attention also outperforms forward log-linear attention on seven of eight downstream retrieval tasks, including question answering and information extraction.

Abstract:We study a non-stochastic contextual bandit problem with Lipschitz losses. At every round, the learner observes the context then picks two actions, observes the difference between their losses, and incurs their mean. The aim is to minimize the regret against a generic non-parametric comparator class of policies mapping contexts to actions; for example, Lipschitz policies and Hölder-smooth policies. We show how relying on a hierarchical discretization technique allows us to improve upon the regret rates achievable under one-point feedback, and even recover the full-information rate in some cases; notably, for sufficiently smooth policy classes or low-dimensional instances. Additionally, for Lipschitz policies, we present an algorithm whose per-round computational complexity is only logarithmic in the time horizon.

[LG-152] Supercharging Olmo-core for Efficient and Scalable MoE Training WWW

作者: Tianhua Tao,Akshita Bhagia,Dirk Groeneveld,Pete Walsh,Tyler Romero,Yashas Samaga,Jacob Morrison,Iz Beltagy,Taira Anderson,Noah A. Smith,Hannaneh Hajishirzi

Abstract:Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models add parameters without proportionally increasing per-token compute. However, training cost also depends on bytes moved, memory held, and kernels launched, and many of those costs follow total parameter size rather than active compute. On infrastructure built for dense models, this mismatch is costly: in early baselines, throughput fell as stored expert parameter size grew, even though the useful work per token stayed nearly fixed. To close this gap, we present a redesigned training stack in Olmo-core, built for efficient, scalable MoE training. We replace the Fully Sharded Data Parallel (FSDP) of earlier Olmo-core versions with an architecture built on Distributed Data Parallel (DDP), and add Expert Parallelism (EP), Pipeline Parallelism (PP), a distributed optimizer, and activation recompute. We propose NVSHMEM-based rowwise EP, which writes each token directly into its expert’s buffer, avoiding dispatch and combine permutation overhead. We make EP fully synchronization-free by keeping routing metadata on the GPU and using device-scheduled grouped GEMMs. Closely integrated MXFP8 cuts compute, activation-memory, and transport costs, and topology-agnostic checkpoints let the parallel layout change between runs. On NVL8 B300 nodes, the stack supports training configurations from 12.9 billion to 1.2 trillion total parameters on up to 512 GPUs, reaching 858 useful-model TFLOP/s/GPU at 1.2 trillion with MXFP8 and per-layer recompute; an experimental capacity test with the optional DeepEP v2 backend reaches 2.38 trillion. We also explain each design choice and share findings for other training systems; for example, we identify a failure pattern we call Token Gerrymandering, in which the MoE router can learn to hack the load-balancing loss, and find that overlapping communication with computation can slow the overlapped kernels by more than it hides.

Abstract:The k -center problem is a fundamental formulation for metric clustering. However, its min-max objective is highly sensitive to outliers, motivating the Robust k -Center (R k C) formulation which permits excluding up to z points as outliers. Existing algorithms for R k C suffer from scalability issues: LP rounding relies on fractional relaxations that scale poorly, known combinatorial approximation algorithms are computationally expensive due to radius guessing, and scalable randomized heuristics require exponential trial multipliers to guarantee success. We present OverclusterDRG, a deterministic, LP-free heuristic for R k C. The algorithm leverages the theoretical insight of farthest-point oversampling – adding exactly z extra candidates to the center set to absorb outliers – followed by a forward-greedy initialization and a 1 -swap local search. Evaluations across real-world datasets show that OverclusterDRG attains a mean approximation ratio of 1.147 against fractional LP lower bounds on the UCI Adult dataset, outperforming state-of-the-art baselines in both clustering quality and speed. By avoiding subset-guessing and exponential trial multipliers, it scales smoothly to n=10^5 points where LP solvers and theoretical algorithms become intractable. Abstract:We propose a privacy-preserving selection layer for collaborative population stratification workflows, enabling an honest-but-curious server to recommend a strong clustering algorithm-hyperparameter configuration from privacy protected shares. Instead of using a fixed workflow such as PCA followed by K-Means with a preset number of clusters, the framework compares multiple clustering methods and parameter settings under privacy constraints. To avoid relying on a public reference basis, we construct a shared low-dimensional representation through a distributed-PCA (DPCA) procedure in which each party computes local top- r principal-component information and the server aggregates only low-rank summaries to recover a global basis. Building on this representation, the framework supports three LDP-protected pipelines: PCA then Noise, Noise then PCA, and Noise-Only. The server evaluates clustering methods and parameter settings using internal validation metrics and recommends a top-performing configuration from the perturbed data; this step is pure post-processing. Experiments on openSNP and 1000 Genomes show that the server-side selection layer reliably identifies strong settings from LDP-protected data. Across both datasets, the PCA-based pipelines outperform Noise-Only in clustering utility, communication cost, and runtime, and show lower membership-inference attack (MIA) power at small privacy budgets. Overall, they provide the best utility–scalability trade-off in our setting. Abstract:Foundation models pretrained on raw transaction sequences are proposed for credit, fraud and churn modeling, with reported gains over gradient boosting, but the data and baselines behind these gains are rarely public. We measure how much the pretraining and adaptation recipes of these models add to a baseline of point-in-time window aggregates and LightGBM, and we propose TBS (Temporal Boosting-Sequence ensemble), which averages the ranks of a boosting model enriched with label-free event-transition features and of a pretrained sequence network fine-tuned jointly with the aggregates. On a synthetic credit-card dataset, the public MBD-mini banking dataset and two proprietary datasets of trade credit and B2B churn, we compare 27 methods at three label budgets with five seeds and paired bootstrap intervals, using sequence models of about 0.4 million parameters pretrained per dataset. Frozen self-supervised embeddings rarely improve the baseline, and a fine-tuned sequence network alone clears it in 9 of 21 target-budget cells. TBS clears it in 19 of 21 cells (18 after FDR adjustment), with a median gain of +1.8 AUC points, and the controls suggest that combining boosting with the pretrained network is the main source of the observed gain. Gains shrink as labels grow and with rich tabular data: with both, the gain on the proprietary datasets is +0.7 and +0.8 points, the latter with an interval including zero. We also re-examine two benchmarks. On IBM TabFormer, the test follows a change in the fraud pattern and the published baseline has no history; with the training period the vendor states, our history-aware LightGBM and our own foundation model stay below the published scores of a commercial model. On IBM AML, a simulation artifact lets a date rule reach F1 0.482, and a point-in-time LightGBM reaches the F1 of graph neural networks whose test graph includes later transactions.

[LG-156] Quantifying Membership Inference Risks in Genomic Data Sharing: The Role of Attackers Auxiliary Information

作者: Maryam Ghasemian,Lynette Hammond Gerido,Erman Ayday
类目: Cryptography and Security (cs.CR); Machine Learning (cs.LG)
*备注:

点击查看摘要

Abstract:Genomic data sharing is essential for biomedical research but introduces significant privacy risks, including membership inference attacks, in which an adversary determines whether a specific individual’s data was used in a study. Existing privacy protections are typically applied after a release format has already been chosen, leaving researchers without a principled method to assess dataset-specific risk beforehand. We propose a server-assisted, principal component analysis-based pre-release auditing framework that maps genomic data into a shared low-dimensional space, applies epsilon-local differential privacy via the Laplace mechanism with a formally derived sensitivity for principal component analysis scores, and estimates membership inference attack power at a controlled 5% false-positive rate using a distance-threshold attack. A membership-neutrality diagnostic based on Unbiased Reconstruction Robustness is reported alongside attack power, precision, and recall. Experiments using the openSNP and 1000 Genomes Project datasets across multiple dimensionalities and privacy budgets show that separation between the researcher’s dataset and public auxiliary data in principal component analysis space is a dominant determinant of attack success, exceeding the effect of perturbation level alone. Comparison against a genome-wide association study-style likelihood ratio test baseline further contextualizes the measured risk. This framework enables researchers, data repositories, and institutional review bodies to quantify dataset-specific membership inference risk before genomic data publication, supporting more informed and privacy-aware biomedical data-sharing decisions.

Abstract:Speech tokenizers convert audio into discrete units, enabling language models to process and generate speech. The goal is to learn compact, text-like representations while preserving enough detail to reconstruct a speaker’s voice and delivery. We propose Facto: a factorized tokenizer that disentangles time-varying information (content and prosody) from static components (speaker identity and recording conditions). We build on a recent linear factorization method for self-supervised features, extending it to handle unseen speakers. Then, we cluster the factorized space and train a lightweight decoder to reconstruct audio from the resulting tokens. By removing the static components before clustering, our tokens are more robust to small noise perturbations. We validate this by testing token stability under various noise conditions. Next, we theoretically analyze Facto’s convergence and scaling properties, quantifying how the factorization improves with the number of training speakers. Finally, we evaluate Facto on a range of downstream tasks. We show that greater token stability translates into improved text-to-speech performance and competitive results in voice conversion and spoken language modeling. Abstract:Self-supervised learning (SSL) results for intensive care unit (ICU) time series are hard to compare when data processing, encoders, and adaptation vary together. We present SLICES, a benchmark and evaluation framework for comparing and extending SSL methods under a shared clinical setup. It fixes 24-hour value and observation-mask inputs, a Transformer encoder, patient-level splits, four endpoints, two adaptation protocols, and five matched seeds across MIMIC-IV, eICU-CRD, and their pooled union. Among these objectives, MAE leads mean AUPRC in all nine frozen classification comparisons, also under converged probes, and in seven of nine fine-tuning comparisons. Fine-tuned MAE leads hospital mortality at full labels and scores higher than a supervised Transformer of the same architecture at every label fraction, and SSL fine-tuning gives the lowest length-of-stay error. Supervised baselines remain strong elsewhere: GRU-D leads 24-hour mortality and XGBoost leads acute kidney injury in all three regimes. Rankings depend on the adaptation protocol, the comparator set, and whether the probe loss matches the metric. Abstract:Generating a token with a language model requires a fixed amount of arithmetic, whose energy sets a floor beneath any hardware. For Qwen3-1.7B at a 16K-token context, gate-level measurements at 5 nm place this floor at 0.89 mJ per token, yet an NVIDIA B300 spends 391-1,120x that. The excess is the price of generality, software layers, programmable hardware and moving weights and key-value (KV) caches from external memory, and it widens with each process generation. We present a co-design approach that brings token generation close to this floor and then lowers the floor itself, optimizing silicon and model together in a gate-level search loop. Fixing one model architecture in the datapath, with weights still loadable, and holding weights and every conversation’s KV cache on-die, a pre-silicon 5 nm design brings an unchanged Qwen3-1.7B token to 3.4x its floor. Co-designing the model with the circuits at fixed quality lowers the floor to 0.29 mJ and the token to 0.52 mJ, 1.8x the new floor and less than the baseline model’s arithmetic alone, while on-die capacity grows from one user to twelve. Against a measured B300 serving the same twelve users, the design decodes each user’s tokens 110x faster at 690x lower energy. To show that one fixed architecture can serve, as a co-processor, the latency-critical workloads around a frontier model, we introduce Polyglot-DC (1.7B and 4B, each with its own design), specialized for each job by distillation and task-specific training into its own weights. As a drafter it speeds single-user speculative decoding of large open models by up to 6.6x at the maximum reasoning effort. Its guard returns multilingual verdicts in a millisecond or less, within a point of the strongest open guard. Its agent and financial-reasoning models lead comparable open models on established benchmarks, with a reasoning turn falling from seconds to tens of milliseconds.

Abstract:There is growing interest in using CGM for purposes other than those initially intended. The results of the external validation indicate that the prior work generalizes well: the performance of each x -hr set of motifs on the external validation set is almost identical to that obtained for \Omega . Abstract:World models develop internal simulators that can learn the structure and dynamics of an environment. It has been demonstrated that their internal representations are both meaningful and causal, but are these representations faithful to the governing dynamics of the environment they are learning? We introduce Anchored Recovery Certification (ARC), a procedure that utilizes a discrete Fréchet distance calculation with ground truth to evaluate dynamical consistency on candidate world models up to an affine gauge. We use the procedure on TD-MPC2 (decoder-free world model) that has learned the pendulum swing on an observation lift under varying hyperparameters at k = 5, 10, 25 steps. The model is then steered within a PCA-derived intervention subspace and compared against a ground-truth simulator using relative error to investigate dynamical faithfulness. ARC sufficiency held for TD-MPC2 most consistently at k = 10, with six of seven constraints statistically significant after Holm-Bonferroni correction, while the relative error between the simulator and the causal latent remained substantial. Further research could be conducted with decoder world models such as DreamerV3 (reconstruction loss) to investigate whether the results differ.

Abstract:Random Forests (RFs) offer strong prediction performance but are difficult to interpret. Most representative trees (MRTs) and artificial representative trees (ARTs) provide surrogate explanations, but a single tree may miss patterns within a forest. We investigate benefits and limitations of clustering-based representative tree ensembles for RF surrogate modeling and assess the contribution of similarity-based clustering relative to random tree partitions. Using linear and nonlinear simulations and regression benchmarks, we evaluate fidelity, prediction accuracy, complexity, and prediction stability against equally sized ensembles of top-ranked MRTs and randomly selected trees. Increasing ensemble size generally improves fidelity, accuracy, and prediction stability. ART ensembles show higher fidelity in simulations and often greater prediction stability for small ensembles. Compared with random tree partitions, similarity-based clustering generally improves ART fidelity in simulations and often on benchmarks. On benchmark datasets, MRT-based ensembles generally achieve higher fidelity and prediction accuracy, whereas ART ensembles have fewer terminal nodes. ART ensembles provide compact surrogates when reduced complexity matters and their fidelity and prediction accuracy meet application requirements. These findings clarify both the trade-offs of representative tree ensembles as RF surrogates and the contribution of similarity-based clustering beyond random clustering.

Abstract:We introduce Actuarial-Informed Neural Networks (AINN), a constrained deep learning framework for sex-specific multi-population longevity forecasting that embeds actuarial knowledge into LSTM training through differentiable penalty terms. Applied to a high-longevity 6-country cluster (Switzerland, Sweden, Norway, West Germany, Netherlands, Japan; 1956-2020), the framework is a challenger to the Li-Lee benchmark and unconstrained neural approaches. Our central finding is that monotonicity constraint intensity lambda functions as a continuous governance dial with a quantifiable accuracy-stability trade-off. At lambda = 0.01, 30-year forecast confidence intervals narrow by 6.5% at zero RMSE cost. At lambda = 0.1, they narrow by 25% at only +0.84% RMSE cost. This trade-off is invisible to standard hyperparameter optimizers, which select lambda by minimizing one-step RMSE, the wrong metric for structural constraints in recursive forecasting. The framework adds three contributions: (i) residual-calibrated process noise that eliminates double-counting in the dual uncertainty framework, reducing confidence intervals by 53-60%; (ii) a 5-seed model ensemble with a coefficient of variation of 1.06%; and (iii) a time-varying credibility weight Z(t) = exp(-alpha t) connecting to Buhlmann credibility theory for blending neural and actuarial predictions. A 10-year out-of-sample backtest (trained on 1956-2010, validated against observed HMD life expectancy for 2011-2020) yields a mean absolute error of 0.38 years, with 11 of 12 country x sex combinations within the 90% confidence interval. The model produces regulatory-grade outputs including Solvency Capital Requirements under the Swiss Solvency Test (ES 99.0%: +1.91 years, CHE Male) and Solvency II, reverse stress testing, and model-based stability verification (amplification ratio 1.02x). [LG-164] Hybrid Compression for Memory-Efficient Matrix-Vector Multiplication

链接: https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.18792
作者: Felipe A. Louza,Giovanni Manzini,Guilherme P. Telles
类目: Machine Learning (cs.LG)
*备注:

点击查看摘要

Abstract:Iterative machine-learning algorithms repeatedly access large real-valued matrices through matrix-vector products, and their performance is limited by memory bandwidth rather than arithmetic throughput. Lossless compression schemes that support computation directly over the compressed data reduce both the data moved and the memory footprint of these workloads. The mm-RePair framework [11] follows this approach by applying the RePair grammar compressor to the Compressed Sparse Row/Value (CSRV) representation of a matrix and performing matrix-vector multiplications directly on the compressed data. Its effectiveness, however, degrades on matrices that are dense or contain many distinct values. In this paper we present a hybrid strategy for the mm-RePair framework that combines grammar and entropy compression. The CSRV sequence is partitioned into a grammar-compressible component, formed by the entries that mm-RePair can compress effectively, and an entropy-compressible component holding the remaining entries, which is encoded with the ans-fold coder [24]. Compression improves further by sorting and delta encoding the entries of each row in the CSRV representation, and by remapping the alphabet to a contiguous range. Experiments on real-valued machine-learning matrices, including word embeddings and transformer hidden states, show that our hybrid strategy is more compact than the original \mmRepair on every input and reduces the peak memory of multiplication, with the largest gains on dense matrices with many distinct values, at competitive multiplication times. It also outperforms the column-reordering variant of \mmRepair on most of the matrices, and combining the two is even more compact on the sparse ones, at the cost of a much longer compression time. Finally, our strategy scales with the number of threads as well as the original \mmRepair does.

[LG-165] Setting Optimal Reserve Prices using Fine-Tuned Language Models

链接: https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.18785
作者: Joshua Foster,Fredrik Odegaard
类目: Machine Learning (cs.LG); Econometrics (econ.EM); Machine Learning (stat.ML)
*备注:

点击查看摘要

Abstract:Online auction houses must set reserve prices for highly differentiated products whose unstructured descriptions contain valuable demand information. Existing approaches generally require managers to specify product attributes in advance. We ask whether a language model can instead learn from listing descriptions and historical bids to set item-specific reserve prices before bidding begins. We fine-tune a pretrained text embedding language model using the structural likelihood of auction bids as its training objective. This directs representation learning toward the valuation distribution that determines the reserve decision. We show that consecutive upper bids identify the tail information needed to set an optimal reserve without observing or modeling the number of potential bidders. A split-sample estimator learns the representation on one half of the data and conducts structural estimation and inference conditional on that representation on the other. We apply the method to approximately 65,800 online used-vehicle auctions. With seller values calibrated to match the sale rate among listings, the model implies a counterfactual net increase of 165.8 million, representing a 14.6% increase above the incumbent reserve policy. The framework translates a listing description and a seller’s value into an item-specific reserve recommendation without constructing a product taxonomy or requiring a bid history for the item being priced. It provides an approach to adapting language models for operational decisions in marketplaces where products are heterogeneous and demand-relevant information is recorded in text.

[LG-166] Can a Vision-Language Model Tune Clustering In Context?

链接: https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.18768
作者: Javith Ranatunga,Paimon Goulart,Evangelos E. Papalexakis
类目: Machine Learning (cs.LG)
*备注:

点击查看摘要

Abstract:Clustering is a widely used unsupervised learning method, but selecting an appropriate algorithm and set of hyperparameters for a specific dataset can require many possible configurations and evaluations. In this work, we investigate whether a Vision-Language Model can instead visually evaluate clustering results and use those decisions to then tune an explicit clustering algorithm. We study this through three progressive experiments using Qwen3.5-27B and five controlled synthetic clustering scenarios. First, we test whether the VLM can distinguish the best clustering result from a pair of plots. Second, we test whether it can assign numerical scores to those plots where a higher score represents a better result. Finally, we use these judgments within an agentic loop in which the VLM scores a k-means clustering and proposes updated hyperparameters that may result in better clustering. Our exploratory results show that the VLM performs well when clear cluster structure is present, while struggling on more ambiguous and noisy settings. In the full agentic experiment, the VLM produces clustering configurations with silhouette scores relatively close to those of grid search and Bayesian optimization, while terminating in much fewer iterations. Overall, these results provide an initial proof of concept that VLM-based visual feedback can be used to autonomously tune an explicit clustering algorithm.

[LG-167] Stagewise Adaptive Boosting
